opus-5.5.text:
Saining Xie: Ha, it really does feel like one of those strange loops in life. When I was applying to the A3 class, which was the special program I was trying to get into back then, the admissions interview was the first time I sat in front of people who weren't just checking whether I could solve problems. They wanted to know how I thought, and what I was curious about. I was a kid. I didn't really know what research was. I just knew I liked figuring out why things worked.

What I remember most is that the conversation kept drifting toward mathematics as a way of seeing the world, not just as a subject you get graded on. Applied math, modeling, the idea that you could take something messy and real and find structure in it. At the time I didn't think much of it. It was just an interview, and I was nervous.

Many years later I ended up at NYU, at Courant, which is one of the most famous places in the world for exactly that kind of thinking: math that touches reality. When I walked into that building I had this odd sense of closure, as if the question that interview had planted in me had finally brought me to the place that embodies the answer. I'm not someone who believes too much in fate, but when the starting point and where you land rhyme that closely, it's hard not to call it a predestined connection.

And honestly, it reminds me that the small moments when you're young, a single conversation, someone taking your half-formed curiosity seriously, can quietly set your direction for decades. You only see the line connecting the dots when you look back.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the A3 interview focused on mathematics and that Xie later attended NYU’s Courant Institute, but never says Richard Courant came up in the interview.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: It's a funny thing, actually. Back when I was an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong, I was in the ACM class—what people call the A3 class—and part of the admissions process was an interview. I remember one of the interviewers asked me a question that, looking back, was really a Courant-style question. It was pure math, very abstract, about function spaces and convergence, nothing to do with programming at all. At the time I had no idea where it came from. I just thought, this is a strange question for a computer science class.

Years later, when I was being interviewed for the faculty position at NYU, I was sitting in a room at Courant, and I suddenly realized the whole flavor of that place—the way people there think, the emphasis on rigor, on analysis, on getting the fundamentals right—was exactly what that one question had been testing. And then I found out that the professor who designed part of our admissions interview had actually spent time at Courant. So in some sense, Courant had been evaluating me before I even knew what Courant was.

I don't believe in fate in a mystical way, but I do think there are these threads in your life that you only see in retrospect. That interview was one of the first moments I was pushed to think about computing not just as building things but as something with real mathematical structure underneath. And that is very much the spirit of Courant—it's a math institute first, and computer science grew out of that soil. When I joined, it felt less like arriving somewhere new and more like closing a loop that had opened fifteen years earlier.

You don’t see those connections while they’re happening; it’s only afterward that they start to feel like fate.
